title: What Bill Campbell Taught Me About Leadership: Q&A at the Campbell Trophy Summit
summary: At the Bill Campbell Trophy Summit, Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi shares leadership lessons on empathy, culture, AI, resilience, and building high-performing teams inspired by Bill Campbell's legacy.

- What Bill Campbell Taught Me About Leadership: Q&A at the Campbell Trophy Summit


It was an honor to join this year’s Bill Campbell Trophy Summit at Stanford University alongside an incredible group of leaders and Campbell Trophy scholars.


The Summit brings together the nation’s top scholar-athletes, nominees for the William V. Campbell Trophy, alongside leaders and friends who were shaped by Bill Campbell’s legacy, including Intuit’s former Chairman and CEO Brad Smith. Its mission is to share hard-won lessons in leadership and life, and in doing so, foster the kind of personal growth and empowerment that Bill spent his career championing.


I had the privilege of discussing these ideas with Pat Gallagher, former president of San Francisco Giants Enterprises. We talked about leading with purpose in the age of AI, why customer empathy matters more than ever, and how the strongest cultures are built on trust, accountability, and a shared commitment to helping others succeed.


I left inspired by the scholars in the room, whose accomplishments extend far beyond the football field. Their curiosity, character, and commitment to making a positive impact give me great confidence in the next generation of leaders.


Thank you to the National Football Foundation, Stanford, and everyone who made this year’s Summit possible. It was a privilege to be part of such a meaningful event.


---


**Pat:** My name is Pat Gallagher, and I’m going to offer up some softball questions, and then we’re going to have a conversation. So you can kind of pretend you’re eavesdropping on a conversation between two people who actually knew Bill well and try to give you a flavor for it. I’ll start with this: Bill believed in people and products. What was the most important thing you took away from Bill that he taught you by example?


**Sasan:** First of all, everything I share up here isn’t just what I learned from Bill, but frankly Bill and Brad because I lived a lot of my life at Intuit when Brad was there, through his lens and Bill’s lens. I’d say the biggest thing I learned was: people don’t care what you think until they know you care about them.


That’s probably the most profound learning for me, because I’m driven, competitive and at the end of the day, everything comes down to people. That’s the single biggest thing I got from Bill, and it’s something Brad modeled every day, so I could see what that looks like, what it means. The more people know you care about them, the more you can create a culture where that person and the team can be the best they can be. It’s something I work on every single day, and it’s probably the single biggest thing.


**Pat:** Bill set a great example for everybody. Intuit today is a much different company, in a much different environment than when Bill started there. But one of the things Bill had and I want to ask about this, is the value of empathy, and how you carry that with the massive number of employees and customers you have now. Talk a little bit about the value of empathy, because that’s something I learned from Bill, and I think he passed it along to all of us.


**Sasan:** The biggest learning around empathy was: how do you have empathy for customers, and how do you have empathy for employees? Starting with our founder, Scott Cook, and of course carried forward by Bill, we believe in a few things we try to role-model every day, and in how we behave. One is our values and we have five, but the essence of one is “Stronger Together,” which is really about valuing and having empathy for everybody’s perspective. Diversity of thought, diversity of perspective, understanding where the other person is coming from and that matters a lot for the products you build, because in our world, winning is about building great products that people use, and use better and more than they use others’. That’s how we win.


Empathy for an individual matters because it’s about how they bring out the best of themselves. And when you have a team that can bring out the best of themselves, they can represent the diversity of the customers you serve in the products you build. That’s something that runs from our founder Scott, to how Bill role-modeled what matters most. And again, I learned a lot of this through the eyes of Brad, because that’s how he taught us to think about empathy for both employees and customers.


## **Winners Keep Score: Building a Culture That Lasts**


**Pat:** Leaders find different ways to drive performance. My impression of Bill was — how do you instill loyalty, belief, and establish culture? That’s one of the things I remember vividly about Bill as a friend. Tell me how you create loyalty, culture, and value.


**Sasan:** I’d start here: winners keep score. You have to be clear about how you’re keeping score. For us, that means: one, how are we doing building a high-performance culture and there are specific things we measure, because at the end of the day it’s all about the team’s performance. Two, we have customer goals, and — similar to sports, though sports are more black-and-white — are you winning versus others? That’s ultimately a key metric that drives whether you deliver for your shareholders.


I start there because culture, for us, is an outcome of how we behave every day and the things you do when nobody’s looking. By being clear about what winning looks like, and clear about the behaviors we expect — one is courage: being bold and fearless, with a bias for action. The second is customer obsession: being obsessed with the benefit customers care about, sweating the details of what you deliver for them. The third is “Stronger Together” and it’s all about people, all about diversity of perspective, being open to debate and even conflict, because great teams don’t always agree on everything, but they debate to get to the best outcome.


And then the last piece is our mission, which, by the way, Brad put in place when he was CEO, and seven and a half years later it’s still the core of what we do: powering prosperity around the world. When we wake up every day, we want to power the prosperity of everyone around us, because it creates economic value. We deal with people’s money. It’s the combination of all of these things that creates the culture we want. And to be clear, it’s never a destination, it’s a work in progress every single day, and you have to keep reinventing yourself, especially as fast as the environment around us is changing.


## **Why Leaders Can’t Sit AI Out**


**Pat:** Shifting gears, I’ll throw out a question you deal with every day, from both a leadership and a culture perspective: AI. The fear of it, but also the opportunity. How do you lead through a period where something only the “nerds” were talking about 15 years ago is now what everyone’s talking about?


**Sasan:** First of all, it’s profound and everybody knows that. I remember, right when I had the privilege of following Brad, about eight years ago, we said, “AI is going to be bigger than the internet and electricity.” Most of us weren’t around when electricity was invented, but think about the internet: if it didn’t exist, you wouldn’t know what to do with yourself. How you communicate, how you buy things, how you interact, it’s all because of the internet. So when you think about the global innovation and economic value of electricity and the internet, it’s profound. And more than eight years ago, we said AI would be bigger than both and that was long before generative AI.


So to your question, I don’t think we’ve seen yet what’s even possible. We’re working on cutting-edge technology with LLM partners — not just within Intuit, but with Anthropic, with OpenAI — we get access to their cutting-edge work because of the partnerships we have. It’s already happening today, but I’d tell you the use of AI right now is probably one or two percent of what it will be. You may be on Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, whatever you use, but the possibilities we’ve tapped are less than one percent. It will change everything, from how we think about machines and automobiles to healthcare. I think we’ll reach a world where, if you allow it, as humans you’re mostly just approving decisions, and all the work is being done for you.


That’s all context and by the way, it could happen sooner than we think, or later than we think. What I’d say to you is: embrace it. What does that mean? If you’re not using Claude, start using it. Go out of your comfort zone, and embrace what it can do for you and learn. Treat it like a brilliant human, or a brilliant team of humans.


I’d say the second thing, our job as leaders is to embrace the possibilities. Talk of “50% of people are going to lose their jobs in three years” creates fear, it creates uncertainty. Will our jobs change in three to four years? A hundred percent. It’s already changing today. But our job as leaders is to embrace what’s possible, embrace how we can change the world, embrace the fact that we can be change agents and shape the future.


I’ll end where I started: embrace it. If you’re not embracing it in your everyday life, whether it’s medical advice, financial decisions, or working through a tough situation with your partner, embrace these tools, because the future is profound and hasn’t even started yet. Don’t be left behind. Lead the change.


## **Advice for Anyone Standing at the Base of Their Climb**


**Pat:** Everyone in this room is here for a reason and I’d call you the farm system, folks who’ve risen to a level where you’re just waiting to find your own way. One of Bill’s strengths was the one-on-ones he’d do with people, sometimes painful. We won’t talk about the profanity part, but that was part of it. When Bill used profanity, it didn’t sound like profanity and we kind of wondered if, when he got to heaven, he could make the Lord take His own name in vain. It’s possible.


If you were sitting one-on-one with these folks, people who are right in the middle of their own climb, just getting started, what advice would you give? What should they be thinking about that maybe they haven’t thought about yet?


**Sasan:** Great question. I’ll share what I tell interns, my own team, and myself. First: don’t ever let anyone tell you what you can’t do. Everything starts with you, set the highest dreams and aspirations for yourself, and don’t put a ceiling on yourself, because if you do, I can assure you everyone else will put an even lower ceiling on you. Dreams are free. So have one, and be bold about it.


Second, if you really want to achieve that dream, whether you achieve it or not is less important than the grit, resilience, and hard work you put in. People ask, “How do I get to your position?” and I say, “Hard work.” “Okay, but how do I really get there?” “No, it’s hard work.” Everyone wants to be great until they find out what it takes to be great. You need grit and perseverance which, by the way, everyone in this room already has.


Third and I’ve only learned this over time, my biggest mistakes, my biggest failures, the biggest pain I’ve endured, have been my biggest life lessons, as long as I got up the next morning and chose to do something about it. Sometimes pain and mistakes don’t get solved overnight, sometimes it takes years.


Big dreams — don’t put a ceiling on yourself; if you can already see exactly how you’ll achieve it, it’s probably not big enough. Grit, perseverance, hard work, as long as you learn from it, because then you understand what “good” really feels like and looks like. That’s the advice I give myself, every single day and now I’ve passed it on to you, for whatever it’s worth.


## **A Good Antidote to Failure**


**Pat:** Scholar-athletes deal with failure in some form and as an athlete, you learn to dust yourself off and get back in there. Is there a lesson about failure, from your own experience or from people you’ve coached — what’s a good antidote to failure? How do you recover from it?


**Sasan:** I overuse sports analogies at work. I get feedback that I should use other examples, but I start with sports because everyone in this room has been through it in some form. If you’re a high-level athlete, you work hard every day, then you get a knee injury, need surgery on your ankle, and you’re out. In sports, the goal line is very clear — win the championship. You get coached every single day; five people start, three come off the bench — perform, you keep playing; don’t perform, you’re on the bench; don’t perform, you’re off the team. The coaching, the scoreboard, what winning looks like, the competition — it’s intense at the college and pro level, in any sport.


That’s why I respect everyone in this room and what you’ve gone through in different aspects of life, not just sports. Self-talk is really important, not just coaching others, but coaching yourself — using sports as an analogy, using my own failures as examples of what you have to do to get up and figure out how tomorrow is going to be better, and just keep working it.


The last thing I’ll say: once you make it to whatever “the top” is for you, and then you fall — you look up at the top of Mount Everest and think, “I don’t know how I’m going to get back up there.” I don’t think you can deal with adversity that way. You have to say, “I’m going to get back to the top, but tomorrow I’m going to put one foot in front of the other. The next day, one foot in front of the other.” Why? Because you believe in you. Because you have a dream, and grit and perseverance, and you’re willing to make pain and suffering your friend. Embrace it. Many people struggle with that, and you can set yourself apart by doing it and also teach others what that looks like.


## **What Bill Would Say Today**


**Pat:** One final question, and then I think we have time for the room. Imagine our buddy Bill was sitting here with us today. I can feel his presence every time we talk about him. Bill didn’t live through the pandemic; I wonder how he would’ve done with Zoom — my guess is he’d have resisted it, because you can’t hug anybody over Zoom. If he were sitting here right now, what do you think he’d want to tell this next generation of leaders?


**Sasan:** It’s hard to replicate what Bill would’ve said, he was one of a kind. The advice he once gave me was: be clear about your “why” in life. Be clear why you exist and what you’re trying to do. Be the change agent, and be the change you want to create. And just get after it, with a few F-bombs.


That’s his advice, which Brad role-modeled for years. I learned a lot of what Bill stands for through Brad, because when you see somebody actually living it, you know what it looks like — which is why I admire Brad so much. That’s what I heard from him, and what I’ve watched him role-model for years. And that’s the advice I’d give all of you.


**How I Spend My Time as CEO — and Why Winning Is My ‘Why’**


**Audience Member:** Can you tell me a little more about what you do for work? And then I want to ask you — what’s your “why”?


**Sasan Goodarzi:** Intuit helps people manage their money. We help businesses grow and run their business with our products. Things like managing cash flow, finding and keeping profitable customers, and knowing how to invest their money. And we do the same for consumers, helping you with… and I thought, “Well, that’s a pretty easy, straightforward job.” And what goes around comes around.


This job, what I do, I try to spend about, depending on the situation, 30 to 40% of my time on customers and product, because that’s how we win: great product. Really understanding, meeting with customers, being in product reviews, looking at our indicators and KPIs, and making sure we’re doing better relative to others because our scoreboard isn’t just internal to what we say we’re going to do, it’s a competitive world.


The second is probably 30 to 40% on people and talent — are we set up as an organization? We have 15 to 16 thousand employees and multiple layers of management, and just like on a sports team, you have to make sure everybody’s focused on the goal line and going in the same direction. That takes a lot at our scale — a lot of time on talent and succession planning, who’s going to be the next person to replace me, someone better than me. So 30 to 40% on people and culture, because winning in the market comes down to people and a winning culture.


And then the third and these percentages aren’t representative of my actual calendar, it’s somewhat situational, about 20% is spent in sessions with other CEOs and thought partners to learn from them, or meeting with our shareholders. So that’s how I spend my time.


My “why” is winning. I love helping our teams create a culture of winning. I love making sure our products are better than other folks’. It’s always been my “why” in life, and it’s what drives me.


**How to Build a Team of Great People**


**Audience Member:** So you talked about the people-first mentality. How do you position your team, and then how do you position yourself among great people?


**Sasan:** The question was: given that teams and people are so important, how do you surround yourself with the right folks? A couple of things we look for: one, the mentality that you want to win. At the end of the day, grit and perseverance to work through tough issues day after day requires you to love the notion of winning — that’s what I look for daily with my own team. How are they dealing with tough issues?


Two, you have to create followership. As a leader, while building the right team, you have to create a followership where people want to go through the wall for the end goal.


And third, you have to be great at your craft. If you’re an offensive lineman, you can’t play quarterback — you’ll get crushed, or vice versa. If you need a great leader in product, you’d better find a great product leader. But it starts with the winning mindset, the winning culture, the followership, and being great at your craft.


And I’d add: things are moving so fast that reinventing yourself, and helping your team reinvent itself — being open to changes, mobility moves, whatever it takes — is really important, because the environment is moving so fast. Being agile is critically important.


**From Star Performer to Leader: Learning to Let Go**


**Audience Member:** Following up on being great at your craft — early in a career you usually get promoted because you’re very good at what you did. Any advice for when you get to a point where you can’t execute with a thousand people? How do you go from being great at your craft to helping others be great, without just rolling up your sleeves and doing it yourself every time?


**Sasan:** Great question. What I’ve learned: one, at any point in your career, but particularly early on, don’t get stuck in one area or one craft. Move to different roles, jobs, and challenges, because it helps you understand the perspective of others. If you’re a designer, I’d actually encourage you not to just be a designer for 20 years and then try to become a design leader — seek different roles, because that helps you diagnose, ask questions, influence, and understand others’ perspectives.


One of my biggest learnings: I left Intuit and came back, and Brad was kind enough to take me back. When he said he’d bring me back, I asked for the CIO job. I had no business being a CIO, no experience at all. Shockingly, Brad said okay. I learned more from that job than any other, because I went way outside my comfort zone to learn how to influence things across the company I didn’t control.


That’s really the point. Different experiences teach you to focus on the goal line rather than what you can control. Most leaders, myself included early on, feel like if they can’t control everything, they can’t get the job done. But nobody controls everything. Those mobility moves teach you to focus on the goal line, and then to teach — is there clarity of vision, clarity of priorities? Learning how to empower and delegate, but also how to inspect, so you can replicate the greatness you brought as an individual contributor by making the team great.


And it’s a work in progress. Get 360 feedback, ask your manager and your team how you’re doing. Openness and curiosity matter, because you want a learning and curiosity mindset, not a know-it-all mindset. I think that’s the key to success.

## Written by


[Sasan Goodarzi](https://www.intuit.com/blog/author/sasan-goodarzi/)


Intuit is on a mission to power prosperity around the world. Under Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Sasan Goodarzi, Intuit has transformed from a tax and accounting platform company into an AI-driven expert platform company. Intuit's powerful combination of proprietary data, domain-specific AI platform capabilities, and AI-powered human expertise is setting the standard for trusted financial intelligence. Sasan’s leadership and operational effectiveness drives Intuit’s vision to bring together data, AI, and human expertise into a single system of intelligence that does the work for customers. Intuit's platform enables businesses to manage from lead to cash, and consumers from credit building to wealth building, all in one place, so they can make high-stakes financial decisions with confidence.


Since becoming CEO in 2019, Intuit has seen record revenue growth and earned recognition from Fortune, Forbes, Fast Company, and others as a leader in AI innovation and as one of the world's top places to work. In 2026, Intuit was named to Fortune’s Best Companies to Work For and Most Innovative Companies lists, TIME’s Most Iconic Companies, and Newsweek’s Most Trustworthy Companies.


Before becoming CEO, Sasan led Intuit's two biggest businesses – its consumer group and its global business solutions group. His previous roles at Intuit include serving as chief information officer, where he led Intuit’s transformation to the cloud, as well as general manager of Intuit’s ProTax and Financial Services Division.


Sasan is passionate about authentic leadership, driving a culture of speed and growth, and how innovation can solve customers' financial challenges. He regularly writes and speaks about the importance of bringing data, AI and human expertise to consumers, small and mid-market businesses and accountants, so they can make the best financial choices to help them prosper.


Together with his wife, Shirin, Sasan established the Goodarzi Scholarship Grant, a program designed to provide financial assistance to California female technology students of Iranian descent who have migrated to the United States within the last seven years.
